Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a developmental condition that affects a person\'s social interaction, communication, and behavior. Its effects vary from one individual to another, which is why it is referred to as a “spectrum.”
Requires a small amount of assistance in daily activities.
Requires moderate support in communication and behavior.
Requires intensive support in daily living and social interaction.

There is no single cause of ASD, but there are factors that can affect it:
 • Genetic factors or family history of ASD
 • Having certain pregnancy conditions or complications in prenatal development
 • Exposure to certain environmental factors while in the womb.
This app helps parents or caregivers assess the physical symptoms of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder who are unable to speak.
Press the + button on the home screen and enter the child\'s name and age
Carefully observe the child\'s movements, facial expressions, and reactions for 5 minutes.
Select a pain score for each category: Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, and Consolability.
Touch the body diagram where the child feels pain
Write down anything else you notice about the child\'s condition
You will see the overall score and recommendations for care
The r-FLACC is a validated tool for nonverbal children with developmental disabilities. It is used in hospitals and clinics around the world.

"The r-FLACC (revised Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability) is a validated behavioral pain assessment tool designed for nonverbal children, especially children with developmental disabilities such as Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). It assesses five categories of behavior, attitudes, or behaviors. Each is scored from 0-2, for a total possible score of 0-10. "
The child has only minor discomfort. Only minimal comfort measures are needed.
The child has clear pain behavior. Pain relief measures and monitoring are required.
The child is in severe pain. Immediate medical intervention is required. Consult a doctor or go to the nearest ER.

• When there is suspicion of illness. 
 • Before and after pain relief intervention. 
 • Regular monitoring if there is ongoing pain. 
 • When the child's behavior changes
When should you consult a doctor?

Seek medical help immediately if: 
 • Score is 7-10 (Severe pain) 
 • Have fever, vomiting, or diarrhea 
 • There is a visible injury or swelling 
 • The child is not eating or drinking 
 • No improvement in pain relief 
 • Have seizures or difficulty breathing 
 • If you are in doubt about the child's condition
Note: TahanApp is a tool for assessment only, not a substitute for professional medical advice. Always consult a healthcare provider for proper diagnosis and treatment.

TahanApp is a mobile application designed to help primary caregivers assess, monitor, and treat the physical pain experienced by children with Autism Spectrum Disorder who cannot speak. \n\nWe use the culturally validated r- FLACC scale or Revised Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability, which is an internationally recognized tool for pain assessment in children with cognitive impairment.
Local Storage: All your data is stored on your device only. No personal information is sent to the internet or other servers.
No Third-party Sharing: We do not share your information with anyone.
Secure Storage: All passwords are hashed for added protection
TahanApp is a tool for pain assessment only. It is not a substitute for professional medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment.
If the child has severe pain (score 7 – 10) or other alarming symptoms, immediately consult a doctor or head to an emergency room.
For questions or suggestions, please contact your healthcare provider or the development team.
Press the Start a New Assessment button above to get started.
Observe the child and select the score that is closest to his or her behavior over the past 5 minutes.
Occasional grimace or frown, withdrawn, disinterested; appears sad or worried
Frequent to constant frown, clenched jaw, quivering chin; distressed looking face; expression of fright or panic
Normal position or relaxed; usual muscle tone and motion to arms and legs
Kicking, or legs drawn up; marked increase in spasticity; constant tremors or jerking
Lying quietly, normal position, moves easily; regular rhythmic breaths (respiration)
Squirming, shifting back and forth, tense or guarded movements; mildly agitated (head back and forth, aggression); shallow, splinting breaths (respirations); occasional sighs
Arches, rigid, or jerking; severe agitation; head banging; shivering (not rigors); breath holding, gasping, or sharp intake of breaths; severe splinting
Moans or whimpers, occasional complaint; occasional verbal outburst or grunt
Crying steadily, screams or sobs, frequent complaints; repeated outbursts; constant grunting
Reassured by occasional touching, hugging, or \"talking to\"; Can be distracted
Difficult to console or comfort; pushing away caregiver; resisting care or comfort measures
Click on the body diagram where the child feels pain. You can add multiple locations.
Write down anything else you have noticed about the child\'s condition.\n\nFor example: behavior, symptoms, etc. (Optional)

Examples of What to Write 

 • What did you notice about the child's behavior? 
 • Are there any other symptoms? (Fever, vomiting, cough) 
 • When did the illness start? 
 • Did anything happen before the injury? (Tripping, getting into a collision) 
 • What did you do to calm down the child?
• Continue with normal eating, sleeping, and play routine. \n • Offer praise or hugs when the child is doing well. \n • Observe and record the child\'s normal behavior.

• Play or read books, use bubbles or videos to distract the child. 
 • Adjust the child's position, use pillows for extra comfort. 
 • Play calming music or white noise; hold or gently stroke the child's hand. 
 • Stay calm and speak to the child in a soothing voice.

• For infants: kangaroo care or swaddling. 
 • For older children: deep breathing or "blow away the pain," or play to distract their attention. 
 • Use a warm compress for tense muscles or cold for swelling. 
 • Dim the lights and reduce noise. 
 • Stay calm and speak gently.

• Stay within the child's line of sight and speak calmly. 
 • Gently rock or shake the child to calm them down. 
 • Tell stories or imagine their favorite place to distract them. 
 • Ensure the child's safety; prevent self-harm. 
 • Call the doctor or nurse immediately if the pain doesn't decrease.

Module 2: Signs of Autism in Children
Module 3: Things That Can Help for Those Newly Diagnosed with Autism
Module 5: Where to Get Support for Autism
Module 6: Easy-to-Read Information and Videos about Autism

Autism is a condition in which a person may behave, think, and feel things in ways that are different from others. 

People with autism may: 
 • have difficulty communicating and interacting with other people 
 • have difficulty understanding what others are thinking or feeling 
 • feel extremely overwhelmed, stressed, or uncomfortable in bright lights or loud sounds 
 • feel anxious or upset in new situations or social activities 
 • need more time to understand information 
 • repeatedly do or think about the same things

Autism is not an illness or a disease. Being autistic does not mean that you are sick; it simply means that your brain works differently from other people's. 

It is a condition that a person is born with. Signs of autism may be noticed during childhood, or sometimes only recognized later in life. 

Autism is not a medical condition that has a treatment or "cure". However, some autistic individuals may need support to help them in certain aspects of their daily lives.
People with Autism Can Live Full and Happy Lives

Being autistic is not a barrier to having a meaningful and happy life. 

Like everyone else, people with autism have things they are good at and things they may find challenging. 

Being autistic does not mean you cannot have friends, relationships, or a job. However, youmay need additional support or assistance in these areas.
Autism is Different for Every Person

Autism is a spectrum, which means that each person with autism has different experiences and abilities. \n\nSome autistic individuals need little to no support, while others may require daily assistance from parents or caregivers.

Some people use different terms to refer to autism, such as: \n • Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) – the medical term used to describe autism. \n • Asperger\'s (or Asperger Syndrome) – a term some people use to describe autistic individuals who have average or above-average levels of intelligence.
The Exact Cause of Autism Is Not Yet Fully Known

It is not yet certain what truly causes autism, or whether there is a single cause. 

Autism can sometimes be seen among family members, which suggests that it may, in some cases, be passed down from parents to children. 

Autism is: 
 • not caused by poor upbringing or bad parenting 
 • not caused by vaccines, such as the MMR vaccine 
 • not linked to food or diet 
 • not an infection that can be passed on to other people
People with Autism May Have Different Levels of Intelligence

Some autistic individuals have average or even above-average intelligence. \n\nOthers may have a learning disability. This means they may have difficulty taking care of themselves and may need help with daily activities.
People with Autism May Also Have Other Conditions

Autistic individuals may also have other conditions, such as: 
 • Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) 
 • Dyslexia 
 • Anxiety 
 • Depression 
 • Epilepsy

Signs of autism in young children may include: 
 • not responding when their name is called 
 • avoiding eye contact or not looking directly at the person speaking to them 
 • not smiling back when someone smiles at them 
 • becoming easily upset by certain tastes, smells, or sounds 
 • repetitive movements such as hand flapping, finger flicking, or rocking their body 
 • speaking less than other children their age 
 • little to no pretend play (make-believe play) 
 • repeating the same words or phrases over and over

Signs of autism in older children may include: 
 • seeming to have difficulty understanding what others think or feel 
 • speaking in unusual ways, such as repeating phrases or talking without engaging in back-and-forth conversation 
 • preferring strict daily routines and becoming very upset or anxious when these routines change 
 • having intense interest in specific topics or activities 
 • becoming easily upset when told to do something 
 • having difficulty making friends or preferring to be alone 
 • understanding language very literally (for example, not understanding idioms like “break a leg”) 
 • having difficulty expressing their own feelings

Sometimes autism presents differently in females and males. 

Autistic females may: 
 • mask some signs of autism by imitating the actions and play of other children 
 • avoid or stay quiet in situations they find challenging 
 • appear to handle social situations better 
 • show fewer repetitive behaviors 

Because of this, autism can sometimes be harder to notice or identify in females.

The signs mentioned are not enough to self-diagnose. Many children may show some of these behaviors but that does not necessarily mean they have autism. 

Do not attempt to diagnose on your own. 

If you notice concerning signs, it is important to consult a licensed doctor, such as a pediatrician, developmental pediatrician, or child psychiatrist, for proper assessment and guidance. 

Early recognition and intervention are crucial to support the child's development

People react differently to an autism diagnosis. 

For some, it can be a relief to understand why they or their child think, feel, and act in certain ways. For others, it may come as a shock. 

Try to give yourself enough time to accept and understand the diagnosis. 

Remember: 
 • help and support are available 
 • even if the situation feels difficult now, things can still improve 
 • you or your child remain the same person as before 
 • autism is not a disease or illness that has a treatment or “cure” 
 • autistic individuals have strengths and things they excel at, in addition to areas where they may need support

You may have felt isolated when you or your child were first diagnosed. 

However, there are places and people you can reach out to for support. 

You can get help from: 
 • local support groups 
 • national charities or organizations that provide assistance 
 • other autistic individuals or parents through social media and forums 
 • your school, college, or workplace 
 • your local government 
 • your GP or the autism assessment team that diagnosed you
Listen to the Stories of Others

Some people find it helpful to learn from the experiences of other individuals with autism. 

You can also look for blogs, videos, or books about autism online. 

Important: 

Remember that every autistic person's experience is different. What happened to someone else may not be the same as what you or your child will experience.
Watch Out for Other Health Issues

Autism is not an illness. However, many autistic people have other conditions. 

These may not always be identified during an autism assessment. 

Consult your GP if you have any concerns about your health or your child's health. They can help you access any additional care you may need.

Gaining more knowledge about autism can be helpful for you and your family. 

There is a lot of information available, and it may take time to understand it all. You don't need to read everything at once. 

You can access reliable information from:
Look for information and advice about living with and caring for a child with autism.
How to Help Your Autistic Child in Daily Life?
How to Help Your Child Communicate

• Use your child's name so they know you are speaking to them 
 • Keep your language simple and clear 
 • Speak slowly and clearly 
 • Use simple gestures, eye contact, and pictures or symbols to support what you are saying 
 • Give your child extra time to understand what you said 
 • Ask the autism assessment team if you can get help from a speech and language therapist (SLT) 
 • Try methods that help them communicate, such as Signalong, Makaton, or PECS 
 • Read tips from the National Autistic Society about communicating with your child

• Ask your child too many questions at once \n • Try to communicate in a noisy or crowded place \n • Say things that can have more than one meaning, such as “sort yourself out,” “good luck,” or “under the weather” (figurative expressions)

Anxiety affects many children with autism. It can be caused by not fully understanding what is happening around them, or by feeling misunderstood or not accepted by non-autistic people. 

Try to understand why your child feels anxious. It may be due to: 
 • Changes in routine – preparing your child for any changes, such as moving to a new classroom at school, can help 
 • Difficulty identifying, understanding, or managing their emotions 
 • Noisy or overly bright/colorful environments – taking your child to a quieter, calmer space, such as another room, can help

Some children with autism may display behaviors such as: 
 • Stimming – a type of repetitive movement (for example, hand flapping or finger flicking) 
 • Meltdowns – a complete loss of control due to being overwhelmed or experiencing intense emotions 

If your child shows these behaviors, read the following advice on how to support and manage your child's behavior.

Many children are picky eaters. 

Children with autism may: 
 • eat only foods of certain colors or textures 
 • eat too little or sometimes too much 
 • eat non-food items (called pica) 
 • have trouble choking or gagging while eating 
 • experience constipation, making them feel full even after eating very little 

Keeping a food diary—recording what, where, and when your child eats—can help you notice patterns and common challenges your child may experience.

Many children with autism have difficulty falling asleep or may wake up several times during the night. 

This may be due to: 
 • Anxiety 
 • Sensitivity to light from smartphones or tablets 
 • Problems with the sleep hormone melatonin 
 • Other issues such as hyperactivity or health conditions that affect sleep 

You can help your child by: 
 • Keeping a sleep diary to track patterns and common challenges 
 • Following a consistent bedtime routine 
 • Ensuring their bedroom is dark and quiet 
 • Having them wear ear plugs if this helps 
 • Talking to a doctor (GP) about managing health conditions that interfere with sleep, such as food sensitivities or breathing problems 

If these strategies do not help, contact your autism team to create a sleep plan that supports your child’s rest. 

If your child’s sleep still does not improve, your GP may refer you to a pediatrician or child psychiatrist experienced with autism.
Some children with autism may find it difficult to make friends. \n\nHere are things you can do to help:

• Seek ideas from other parents through autism forums and local support groups 
 • Ask your child’s school how they can provide support 
 • Consult your autism team on how to help your child communicate and interact with others 
 • Look in the National Autistic Society directory for local autism-friendly social groups 
 • Read additional advice about friendship from the National Autistic Society
• Put too much pressure on your child – learning social skills takes time \n • Force your child into social situations if they are comfortable being alone

Sharing your autism diagnosis—or your child’s—with people close to you can help them better understand how to support you. 

They can assist with: 
 • Daily tasks to give you more time to focus on yourself or your child 
 • Providing emotional support
For autistic children and youth, as well as their parents and caregivers.
The assessment team that diagnosed you or your child should provide information about local support groups. \n\nYou can also find local groups through:
A large non-profit organization for families and individuals with autism, with chapters across the country offering family support groups, seminar series, and referral services.
A website and online support resource for parents and families of children with autism in the Philippines, offering information, tips, and resource links.

Many people with autism share their experiences and provide support through forums and social media. 
 • You don’t need to actively participate; reading their posts can be helpful. 
 • A good place to start is with groups run by autism charities. 
 • Important: NHS does not monitor these sites.
Autism Center and Speech Development of the Philippines
Comments on social media and forums are usually based on personal experience and should not be taken as advice guaranteed to help you or your child.

You can request support to make things easier for yourself or your child. 

Check what help is available at: 
 • Nursery or school – speak with teachers or the Special Educational Needs Coordinator (SENCO) 
 • College or university – contact student support services 
 • Workplace – talk to your manager and Human Resources (HR)
You may be able to access support and financial benefits from your local council. \n\nThe type of help available depends on your situation.

There are easy-to-read materials and videos that can help in understanding autism. \n\nThese can be used by parents, caregivers, or even autistic children to better understand autism and how it may affect daily life.
